node.label: Alexandra Walsham
node.date_label: Church Papists 1993 · Providence 1999 · Charitable Hatred 2006 · Disenchantment reassessed 2008 · The Reformation of the Landscape 2011
node.description: In “The Reformation and ‘The Disenchantment of the World’ Reassessed” (2008), Alexandra Walsham argues that cycles of desacralization and resacralization better capture religious change than a linear account of disenchantment. The Reformation of the Landscape (2011) examines how religious change and physical places shaped one another, connecting confessional identities with collective memory. Keith Thomas praised its synthesis in his 2011 review but thought Walsham sometimes too eager to overturn conventional wisdom, questioning both continuing piety at eighteenth-century spas and the extent of Protestant myth-making. With Julia Crick, she also challenged a sharp division between manuscript and print (2004). Her later work treats reused religious objects as agents of memory and investigates how early modern record-keeping shaped the archives historians inherit.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Church Papists: Catholicism, Conformity and Confessional Polemic in Early Modern England (1993); Providence in Early Modern England (1999); The Uses of Script and Print, 1300–1700 (2004), coedited with Julia Crick, including their joint introduction; Charitable Hatred: Tolerance and Intolerance in England, 1500–1700 (2006); “The Reformation and ‘The Disenchantment of the World’ Reassessed” (2008); The Reformation of the Landscape: Religion, Identity, and Memory in Early Modern Britain and Ireland (2011); “History, Memory, and the English Reformation” (2012); Catholic Reformation in Protestant Britain (2014); “The Social History of the Archive” (2016), introductory essay; “Recycling the Sacred” (2017).
node.scope_note: The 2008 and 2012 essays are known here through publisher abstracts and displayed references; the landscape book through its abstract and Thomas’s selected review passages. The 2004 introduction, 2016 archive essay and 2017 material-culture article were read in specified excerpts. Selected monographs, cited theoretical originals, and the rest of the edited collections remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Killing Stones” (2011), Thomas praises Walsham’s The Reformation of the Landscape (2011) but questions its account of continuing piety at eighteenth-century spas.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Review, paragraphs beginning “Its footnotes testify” and “Walsham, who is deeply hostile” (web lines 129, 140–142): praise accompanies “unduly optimistic”. Review passages read; monograph unread. Criticism concerns this interpretation, not the whole book.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Reformation and ‘The Disenchantment of the World’ Reassessed” (2008), Walsham reconsiders the Weberian disenchantment thesis and proposes cycles of desacralization and resacralization in place of a linear narrative.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract, final sentence, read: “cycles of desacralization and resacralization”; opening names Weber. Article body unread. This is the abstract’s stated historiographical intervention, not a fresh reading of Weber or a claim that every part of his sociology is rejected.

proposed_edges.relationship: With Julia Crick, Walsham’s “Introduction: Script, print, and history” (2004) challenges the script-to-print divide associated with Eisenstein’s The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979), emphasizing the media’s continued interaction.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt pp. 3–5, especially p. 4: “lingering co-existence, interaction and symbiosis”. Joint argument, not sole authorship. Eisenstein’s original is unread here; the introduction cites its 1980 edition. Introduction beyond the excerpt unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In their “Introduction: Script, print, and history” (2004), Walsham and Julia Crick use Chartier’s work on readers’ appropriation to question claims that printed texts impose uniform meanings.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt p. 5 and n. 9 read: Chartier “has cast doubt on the uniformity” of print. His cited works include The Cultural Uses of Print in Early Modern France (English translation, 1987). Those works unread; debt belongs to both coauthors.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Recycling the Sacred” (2017), Walsham applies Nora’s lieux de mémoire to repurposed religious objects that sustain remembering and forgetting.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Published article p. 1124 and n. 10 read: “lieux de mémoire”; note names Nora’s 1989 essay. Other resources share the note. Original Nora essay unread for this dossier; application is specific to remodeled objects.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Recycling the Sacred” (2017), Walsham explicitly draws inspiration from Appadurai’s social life of things when connecting human and object histories.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Article p. 1124 and n. 11 read: “Taking inspiration”. Appadurai’s edited The Social Life of Things (1986) is named with Kopytoff and others. No exclusive derivation; originals unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Social History of the Archive” (2016), Walsham names Stoler’s Along the Archival Grain (2009) as an inspiration for investigating the internal logic of archival records.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Accepted manuscript, paragraph beginning “The Social History of the Archive responds” (body paragraph 73), n. 143: “one source of inspiration”. Passage and footnote read; Stoler’s book unread here. Attribution concerns the volume’s method, not adoption of every colonial argument.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “History, Memory, and the English Reformation” (2012), Walsham examines how personal recollection and social memory reshaped remembrance of the Reformation between 1530 and 1700.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract read: “personal recollection and social memory”. Article body unread. Limited to its stated research programme and period; no detailed conclusions inferred.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Recycling the Sacred” (2017), Walsham treats the altered uses and afterlives of liturgical objects as a material history of religious change.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Article pp. 1124–1125, 1154 read; combines textual, material and archaeological evidence. Middle cases unread. Contribution concerns material culture, not a claim about aggregate consumer demand.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Social History of the Archive” (2016), Walsham argues for examining the creation, selection and preservation of early modern records as historical practices that shape knowledge.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Accepted manuscript opening, body paragraphs 4–12, read. Paragraph 8 makes the archive a subject of enquiry; paragraphs 10–11 state the intervention. Rest of collection unread; no claim of sole authorship of the collaborative volume.

proposed_edges.relationship: In The Reformation of the Landscape (2011), Alexandra Walsham contributes to spatial history by treating religious change and the making of landscapes as interacting processes and calling for greater historical attention to place, space and physical environment.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's introduction abstract, together with the book-level abstract and publication metadata. These explicitly describe a reciprocal account of religious change and landscape and a methodological call for attention to space. The chapter body and complete book were not accessible and are unread. This is a bounded contribution to the existing landscape-history component of spatialhistory, not a claim about GIS or the foundation of the field.
